Real-time object detectors are usually reported by mean latency o r frame rate. An availability failure,
however, occurs when a single response misses the application' s deadline. Candidate-inflation latency
attacks drive the number of boxes entering non-maximum suppres sion (NMS) far beyond its clean
range. Recent evaluations report that realistic hardware, represen tations and optimized suppression
reduce the severity of such attacks. Reduced severity is not a bo und: work remains attacker-controlled,
and prior studies do not jointly report deadline-relative tail la tency and deadline-miss ratio for a
defended serving path. We therefore admit at most K candidates to NMS. The selection operation
is standard; new is its use as a deployment-selected bound on a ttacker-controlled work, calibrated

an already
promoted artifact. Replaying identical attacked candidate arra ys through three suppression backends
shows the attack to be strongly implementation dependent, ye t under our principal attack budget no
uncapped backend meets a 30-Hz frame deadline. The bound hold s across two detector geometries
of differing anchor count, three backends, a second evaluation corpus and a thermally throttled edge
board, while the runtime's shipped candidate ceiling meets th e suppression screen on the GPU backend
only. The accuracy the bound costs is measured rather than assum ed. Per-stage instrumentation then
shows that, once candidate handling is bounded, the largest a ttack-associated increment is decode,
not suppression. Bounding suppression work is necessary for dead line integrity but not sufficient.
Keywords: real-time object detection, latency attacks, non-maximum suppression, deadline

Backend choice substantially reduces attacked
suppression latency, but no uncapped backend we
tested satisfies the declared suppression screen.
Following the deployment-realism concern of prior
work [
15, 16], we replay identical attacked can-
didate arrays through three suppression imple-
mentations. Over the same 48 images the sup-
pression call's p95 is 635.35 ms on the deployed
NumPy path, 177.71 ms on torchvision CPU and
49.08 ms on torchvision CUDA. CPU arms use the
host clock. CUDA arms are bracketed by device
synchronization after a warm-up, since an unsyn-
chronized timing measures the kernel launch, not
the work. The host-to-device copy is excluded; at
0.183 ms p95 it changes neither ordering nor ver-
dict, so the CUDA figure understates a backend
fed from the host.
5

Top-K selection is a standard operation and we
claim no novelty for it. What is proposed here is its
use as a deployment-selected bound on attacker-
controlled work, with the value calibrated against
a declared deadline and its accuracy cost mea-
sured. Let C be the candidates surviving the
confidence threshold and N = |C|. Before NMS
we retain only CK = TopK( C, K), admitting for
N > K the K candidates smallest under the
lexicographic key ( −sj, j): argpartition on the
negated scores at index K − 1 locates the cutoff,
every candidate strictly above it is admitted, and
the remaining places go to candidates equal to it in
ascending index order. The tie rule is not a formal-
ity, NumPy's introselect being unstable and exact
ties reachable at fp16 or quantized scores. The cut
is O(N ) and adds no pairwise IoU comparison, the
term Eq. (
4) bounds.

evidence.excerpt:
served deadline
The cap reduces client-side p95 under attack by
a factor of 15.10, a median over five independent
A/B sessions, yet the defended requests still miss
De2e = 33 .3 ms every time. That is no contra-
diction: the work bound applies to suppression,
and TNMS ≤ Dsupp does not imply Le2e ≤ De2e.
Nor is the miss attributable to the attack alone.
Attacked images must be delivered losslessly, since
re-encoding at the quality this pool serves did
not preserve the perturbation, so comparing them
against the JPEG corpus varies two things at once.
We therefore re-encoded the same 48 sources into
the attacked arm's format and served all three
arms through the same pool at the same cap, in
ten sessions of 144 requests at ϵ = 2/255.
The adversary turns out not to be necessary for
the miss. Clean lossless images reach p95 66.20 ms
at a deadline-miss ratio of 0.927, against 61.20

evidence.excerpt:
The anchor grid sets the maximum candidate
count, so a cap validated on one output tensor
says little about another. We repeated the capture
and the sweep on the same detector family with-
out its P2 head: 33,600 anchors against 136,000,
a factor of four in the quantity that sets the
ceiling. K = 1024 holds the suppression budget
on both, 3.11 ms against 4.19 ms in the same
run, while the runtime's shipped ceiling of 30,000
misses on both, at 187.30 and 342.96 ms. This is
suppression replay only; no accuracy claim is made
for the second model, and the bound is estab-
lished for the two geometries tested rather than
for anchor-based detectors in general.

tract. Transfer across input distributions is what

pool serves lossless requests ( §

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The headline suppression-latency reduction is corroborated by objective wall-clock measurements across three independent backends, a second detector geometry, a second corpus, and an edge board, while the accuracy cost is measured on held-out test-dev data.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Client-observed and stage-isolated p95 wall-clock latency, deadline-miss ratio, and held-out COCO-style AP@[.50:.95] on the exported artifact.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent on a differentiable surrogate for pre-NMS candidate count, plus a grid-swept calibration rule selecting K from measured tail latency and an accuracy tolerance.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims match the reported measurements with exemplary precision: the paper shows bounded admission successfully confines NMS tail latency (e.g., to 4.28 ms at K=1024), while candidly demonstrating that end-to-end deadline integrity fails due to input decoding overhead rather than candidate handling.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation is rigorous and multi-faceted, testing multiple anchor configurations, two vision corpora (VisDrone and BDD100K), thermal throttling on an edge platform (Raspberry Pi 4B), and end-to-end client-observed tail latencies with matched lossless image controls.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluations rely on objective physical clock measurements across three distinct backends, edge hardware, and held-out test datasets.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Client-observed and stage-isolated p95 wall-clock latency, deadline-miss ratio (DMR), and held-out COCO-style AP@[0.50:0.95] across multiple independent suppression runtimes and hardware platforms.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent on anchor confidence scores for generating adversarial candidate inflation, and an analytical calibration rule over swept candidate grids to determine the admission bound K*.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly report threats to validity, noting that K* calibration was conducted over limited sessions, that millisecond timings are target-specific rather than formal WCET bounds, and that bounding suppression work is insufficient by itself to secure the end-to-end serving pipeline.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, implementing a deterministic projected gradient ascent attack targeting pre-NMS anchor expansion, replaying captured arrays across three distinct suppression backends (NumPy CPU, torchvision CPU, and torchvision CUDA), and instrumenting both stage-local and end-to-end client latencies.
primary.quality_rationale: This work provides a sound, highly transparent, and realistic systems-level evaluation of latency attacks and defenses in real-time object detection, characterized by honest negative findings regarding end-to-end client deadlines and fully documented artifacts.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper demonstrates that candidate-inflation latency attacks against object detection remain attacker-controlled across backends, and establishes a deployment-calibrated candidate admission bound (K) prior to NMS that strictly limits suppression latency while quantifying its minimal clean accuracy cost.

scholarly_quality.rationale: This work provides a sound, highly transparent, and realistic systems-level evaluation of latency attacks and defenses in real-time object detection, characterized by honest negative findings regarding end-to-end client deadlines and fully documented artifacts.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly report threats to validity, noting that K* calibration was conducted over limited sessions, that millisecond timings are target-specific rather than formal WCET bounds, and that bounding suppression work is insufficient by itself to secure the end-to-end serving pipeline.
